newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia report sees economic doom in S. Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Australia report sees economic doom in S. Pacific.

text.p: A secret Australian government report has warned of impending economic disaster in several South Pacific countries, citing mismanagement and corruption and detailing the personal habits of political leaders.
A 93-page document marked 'AUSTEO', or Australian Eyes Only, said at least one country, tiny Nauru, was on the brink of calamity and in such bad shape it might lose its independence.

The paper was prepared jointly by the foreign ministry and treasury for Treasurer Peter Costello as a briefing for last weekend's summit of economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum in the tropical resort town of Cairns.

It was left on a table in a public area at the summit where it was obtained by Reuters. Australian officials would not comment on the paper or its contents, but a senior official privately confirmed it was genuine.
AUSTEO is one of Australia's highest security ratings, far higher than top secret.

Australia's Labor Opposition, calling the report patronising and contemptuous and warning of diplomatic strife with South Pacific governments, demanded Costello formally apologise to South Pacific nations.

"It is one thing for a confidential briefing paper to give tough-minded and objective assessments -- but this patronising and contemptuous document will take a long time to be forgiven," said acting Opposition leader Gareth Evans, a former foreign minister.
"Treasurer Costello should immediately apologise to the island nations concerned."
Among the dry statistics on economic growth, debt service levels and budget deficits, the paper provided Costello with juicy tidbits about the personal behaviour of some of his guests.

It described what it said were the drinking habits of some of the ministers, including whether they became belligerent or mellow when drunk, along with personal traits, family crises and religious habits.
Some were labelled corrupt -- one was nicknamed 'Mister Ten Percent', another was "corrupt, spurns due process and advice and attracts carpetbaggers".
Others were portrayed simply as incompetent.

Australia and New Zealand are the forum's biggest economies, dwarfing the poorer island nations -- the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.
Most South Pacific economies are afflicted by low growth, high debt, bloated public sectors, growing populations and weak or virtually non-existent private sectors.
"Economic problems are mounting in the South Pacific, but reform is being frustrated by leaders' anxiety about its political costs and uncertainty about its benefits," the briefing said.
"Mismanagement is hurting, with the Solomon Islands, Nauru and the Cook Islands on the brink of insolvency," it said.
"Pacific leaders will continue to flirt with easy solutions to their economic problems, especially quick-fix, easy-money schemes and over-exploitation of natural resources," it said.
"They will find it hard to stop asking others to solve their problems, so they will continue to push for more aid, new trade preferences and easier labour access."
The briefing said Nauru, with a population of 9,000, was in worse shape, despite a once-rich phosphate industry and compensation for phosphate mining from former trustee Australia.
Nauru's financial assets have tumbled to A$200 million (US$147 million) from A$1.2 billion in 1991.
"Financial collapse is imminent, the only question is timing," the paper said.
"Nauru mismanaged its finances with bad investments, instances of fraud and excessive government spending funded by heavy borrowing," it said.
"Nauru is looking down the barrel of being an impoverished and desperate entity unable to sustain its sovereignty."
The paper did not say who might assume responsibility for Nauru, but warned the Australian government it would come under pressure to resettle Nauruans or pay new compensation.
The paper divides the 14 island states into six groups, based on economic and social conditions, with headlines such as "Melanesian mayhem", "Imprudent Micronesians" and "Bottom of the heap".
